Michael Stuhlbarg delivers a towering performance as the oligarch Boris Berezovsky in this gripping political drama.

“Patriots” shines when it releases its need to peacock as a Shakespearean-level epic and gets into some Shakespearean-like complexity.

Though Morgan is plenty perceptive about character, there’s something cool at the center of Patriots that begins to chafe as the play nears its end.
Onstage, it’s a recipe for information overload — a treatment that is both crowded and shallow.
But I wouldn’t generally take “Patriots” as a reliable source of information.
The play's not the thing here; the players are, and Stuhlbarg and Keen are the crème de la Kremlin.
These charmless characters are broadly outlined, psychologically shallow and simplistically played.
Leaning so hard on the relevance of its issues that it pulverizes any actual drama, the show from London is one of the season’s longest sits.
I would advise them all to rush to the Theatre, where Peter Morgan’s “Patriots” is offering one of the most absorbing accounts of political intrigue I’ve ever seen on a Broadway stage.

Featuring brilliant performances by Michael Stuhlbarg as Russian-Jewish businessman Boris Berezovsky and Will Keen, repeating his Olivier Award-winning London performance, as Putin, Patriots is the sort of gripping real-life drama that only makes you want to learn more.

Pulling all this together — with Jack Knowles’ dramatic lighting, Adam Cork’s sound and original music, and Ash J. Woodward’s striking video design — is Rupert Goold. Ever since he startled Manhattan audiences with his 2008. Macbeth, he has never lowered his standards. He has only raised them. Patriots is a new high.

This is but one impressive moment among many in a memorable accomplished performance. The prickly young Berezovsky’s interests soon turn toward wealth and he uses his skills – in a newly relaxed Russia – to become one of the country’s most powerful oligarchs, ultimately owning a prominent television station and exploiting his closeness with Yelt...
As with “The Crown,” “Patriots” is primarily a source of entertainment – and it succeeds in that regard.
The tug-of-war between them is endlessly fascinating and is more than enough reason to check out Patriots.
As a result, “Patriots,” which prizes talk over action, can often feel like a college history class you were forced into taking.

Although Peter Morgan’s telling of the rise of Putin and Russian oligarchs feels a bit oversimplified and leaves most characters one- or two-dimensional, Rupert Goold’s electric direction elevates the material to make history feel like a blur of lights and sound.
In Patriots, his talent bridges a director and writer who are never in sync, finding meaning in Goold’s absurdity and a recognizable person in Morgan’s pomposity.
But while the Broadway production boasts creative stage design, it fails to provide useful insight into the politics of post
Ultimately, the first-rate comedy of the first act turns into the second-rate melodrama of the second act.
Lacking detail and focus, Patriots is a character study without much of either.

Stuhlbarg’s real prowess as an actor was making us like a character who we would ordinarily dismiss, and I do think the uniqueness of his nuanced portrayal is one of the primary factors helping to sell the show.
Patriots is political drama at its most urgent, as relevant as today’s headlines, with a psychological complexity and a dark humor that make it crackling entertainment.

Overall, Michael Stuhlbarg is Tony-worthy as Boris Berezovsky as he captures his conscience in a truly cerebral performance that is equal in excellence to Gary Oldman as Winston Churchill in “Darkest Hour.”
Patriots offers a lesson about recent Russian history whose subject may not be what audiences at the jam-packed end of the current season are looking for.

cn.t: Critics find Peter Morgan's Putin-era drama gripping but lacking depth, with Michael Stuhlbarg's performance as oligarch Boris Berezovsky earning widespread praise while the play itself draws mixed reactions for style over insight.

sg.ra: TickPick and Headout both name Center Orchestra rows E-J (TickPick: E-J; SeatPlan/Headout: F-O) as the prime zone at the Barrymore because the 1,058-seat house is shallow enough that the mezzanine overhang only kicks in at row K of the orchestra, leaving center rows F-J with an uncovered, forward sightline well-suited to the text-driven plays this house tends to book.

Headout and TickPick both warn against Orchestra rows A-C at the Barrymore specifically because the stage at this 1928 house sits high relative to the front rows — TickPick: 'rows A, B, and C are too close to the stage and might block your view'; Headout adds that 'seats closer to the stage may cause neck strain from looking upward.'

SeatPlan and TickPick both confirm the Barrymore mezzanine overhang begins at row K of the orchestra but isn't obstructive — SeatPlan: 'those sitting in the rear of the Orchestra section will notice that the stage feels impressively close'; the house's well-raked orchestra keeps sightlines intact even under cover, which matters because this is a 1,058-seat intimate-play house and losing the rear orchestra would shrink the good-seat pool significantly.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, under premium pricing
sg.ra: SeatPlan directly names row A Center Front Mezzanine as the house favorite at the Barrymore — 'very popular thanks to its fantastic elevated position above the stage' — and both SeatPlan and TickPick emphasize the Barrymore's front mezzanine is only 5 rows deep (A-E, 196 seats), so even row E retains a wide, pitched view and benefits from the intimate 1,058-seat scale.

SeatPlan specifically praises the Barrymore rear mezzanine rake: 'a decent rake means even the back rows offer a surprisingly good look at the stage' and 'even in the far corner theatergoers won't feel too much strain to make out the stage.' The house's three-flights-up rear mezz is the trade-off for the small footprint, but the rake compensates for distance in a way deeper houses don't manage.

Headout and TickPick both flag the Barrymore's six box seats (three per side of the orchestra) and the orchestra rows D-E directly beneath them as compromised — Headout: 'seats under the Boxes in rows D and E a little restricted'; TickPick adds 'far Left and Right Orchestra and the outer corners of the Mezzanine can have reduced sightlines.' This is a specific quirk of the Barrymore's 1928 proscenium layout with built-in side boxes.
